newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grains - Japan shrugs off USDA report.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grains - Japan shrugs off USDA report.

text.p: Japanese traders shrugged off last week's monthly supply-demand report of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) while floods in southern China may damage its rice crop, traders said on Monday.

"Friday's USDA reports were within our expectations. We're watching the firming U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rate for nearby shipments, but feel no urgent need to buy immediately," said a corn trader at a major trade house in Japan.
The USDA's monthly report was given a neutral reception in grain futures markets in the United States.
The USDA said the 1996/97 (Sept/Aug) corn carryover estimate would reach 916 million bushels, above the June forecast for 909 million and well within trade expectations.
In China, floods across the southern part of the country may damage rice crops and cause minor problems for corn output, dealers said.
"Floods in southern and eastern areas will damage rice," a Shanghai-based U.S. grain trader said.
Chinese traders said the price of a 50,000 tonne shipment of Chinese corn bought by South Korea on Monday for about US$151.80 a tonne C&F was higher than expected.
"The $151 a tonne level is much higher than the $125 a tonne we have seen in recent export deals," a trader said.

They blamed the higher prices on expensive shipment specifications requiring corn to be delivered in lots of 5,000-10,000 tonnes to the western North Korean port of Nampo. The shipment was bought on a cost-and-freight basis.

Japanese traders, on the other hand, said Chinese exporters must lower their offer prices of corn to Japanese buyers to around US$110 to $120 per tonne C&F from the current level of $130 a tonne so they can compete with U.S. origins.
"Given quality problem of Chinese corn, local end-users want a further price cut," a corn trader said.

Japanese importers have already covered up to 20 percent of their U.S. corn needs for the last quarter of 1997, traders said. Corn premiums were being quoted at around 98 U.S. cents a bushel over CBOT September futures.
